passages.t: Greeting: the hope God promised before time began
passages.happening:
Paul opens with a long greeting. “Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began” (verses 1-2).

“In His own time He has made His word evident in the proclamation entrusted to me by the command of God our Savior” (verse 3).

“To Titus, my true child in our common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Only Romans has a clearly longer opening among Paul's letters. In a few lines Paul packs in what the whole letter will be about.

He is ‘a servant of God’, a slave who belongs to God, and ‘an apostle of Jesus Christ’, one sent with his message. And his work has a goal: that God's people would believe, and know the truth, and that this truth would lead ‘to godliness’, a life that honours God. Right belief and right living belong together. The false teachers on Crete had the first without the second (verse 16).

Then Paul speaks of hope. God promised eternal life ‘before time began’, before the world was made. And this God ‘cannot lie’. Hold on to that phrase, because a few verses later Paul will quote a saying about Cretans being liars. Whatever the island's reputation, the God of the gospel always tells the truth.

Notice the title ‘Savior’. Paul gives it to God in verse 3 and to Christ Jesus in verse 4. The letter will do this again and again.

Titus is ‘my true child in our common faith’. Titus was a Gentile and Paul a Jew, but their faith is ‘common’, shared. In Christ, Jew and Gentile believe the same gospel and belong to the same family.
passages.ot:
God is the one who keeps his word: “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind. Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill?” (Numbers 23:19).

The promise of blessing for all peoples goes back to Abraham: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). And knowing God, more than anything else, is what the prophets prized: “let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me” (Jeremiah 9:24).
passages.asks: Paul says that true faith leads to godliness. Ask whether what you believe is changing how you live. Ask what it means to you that God cannot lie and has promised eternal life. And ask who shares your ‘common faith’ across lines that once would have divided you, and how you treat them.

passages.happening:
“The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you” (verse 5).

“An elder must be blameless, the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers and who are not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination. As God’s steward, an overseer must be above reproach—not self-absorbed, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not greedy for money. Instead, he must be hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined” (verses 6-8).

“He must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Paul and Titus had worked together on Crete, and when Paul moved on he left Titus to finish the job. The word for ‘set in order’ means to put right what was left undone. The churches existed, but they had no appointed leaders.

So Titus is to appoint elders ‘in every town’. Paul had done the same from his very first missionary trip (Acts 14:23). In verse 7 he calls the same leader an ‘overseer’, so in this letter the two words seem to name the same people.

Read the list slowly and notice what it is about. Almost every item is about character. The overseer is ‘God's steward’, the word for the manager who ran a household on its owner's behalf. He does not own the church. He looks after it for God, and he will answer to God for how he does it.

There are five things he must not be: full of himself, quick to anger, a heavy drinker, violent, greedy. There are six things he must be: welcoming to strangers, a lover of what is good, self-controlled, fair, holy, and disciplined. And there is one thing he must hold: the true message, so that he can both encourage and correct.

His home matters too. In the Roman world a man was expected to run his household, and how his family lived reflected on him. Paul wants a leader whose family life is not a scandal.
passages.ot:
Moses was told to choose leaders by their character: “select capable men from among the people—God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain” (Exodus 18:21). And again: “Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes” (Deuteronomy 1:13).

The prophets condemned leaders who served themselves: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). And Proverbs praises the very self-control Paul asks for: “He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior” (Proverbs 16:32).
passages.hard:
Must church leaders today meet this list, and how do churches read it?

Churches are ordered in different ways, and each reads these verses in its own light. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, and Methodist churches in their own form, are led by bishops who oversee many congregations. Presbyterian and Reformed churches are led by elders who govern together. Baptist, Congregational and many free churches hold that each local congregation, under Christ, chooses its own leaders. These notes do not choose.

Christians read ‘the husband of but one wife’ in several ways: a man faithful in marriage (the Greek says, literally, ‘a one-woman man’), a ban on having more than one wife, a ban on remarriage after divorce, or a rule that leaders must be married. ‘Children who are believers’ can also be translated ‘faithful children’. Some read it as children who profess faith; others as children who are trustworthy and well behaved, as the rest of the verse suggests, since a child's faith is finally beyond a parent's control. Churches also differ on whether the office is open to women, as the notes on 1 Timothy 2 and 3 set out. These notes do not choose.

What every reading shares is that character comes before gifting. A gifted leader who is violent, greedy, harsh, proud or deceitful does not meet Paul's standard, however well he preaches or however much his church grows.

And nothing in this passage shields a leader who does harm. Christians agree that leaders are servants accountable to Christ and to his word, and that no authority may be used to cover abuse. If a leader uses his place to control, exploit or harm, these verses do not protect him. Anyone harmed by a church leader is free to speak to another trusted leader, a counselor, or, where a crime is involved, the authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And if your own children have wandered from the faith, this verse is not a verdict on you or on them. Many faithful parents carry that grief.
passages.asks: Paul asks for leaders whose character can be trusted. Ask what you look for in a leader: gifts and success, or the kind of person Paul describes. If you lead anyone, at home, at work, or in church, ask which of these qualities is weakest in you. And ask whether you pray for the leaders of your church, who carry a heavy trust.

passages.happening: “For many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision, who must be silenced. For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Now Paul says why good elders are so urgently needed. Some teachers on Crete were causing great harm.

Paul describes them in three ways. They were ‘rebellious’, refusing to be corrected. They were ‘full of empty talk’, many words with nothing in them. And they were deceptive. Worse, they were doing it ‘for the sake of dishonorable gain’, teaching for money.

‘They undermine entire households.’ Remember that the churches met in homes. A teacher who won over one household could unsettle a whole congregation. Whole families were being turned upside down.

‘Those of the circumcision’ were most likely Jewish believers in Jesus, or teachers close to them, who insisted that Gentile believers keep parts of the law to belong fully to God's people. Verse 14 mentions their ‘Jewish myths’ and ‘the commands of men’, and verse 15 suggests rules about what was clean and unclean. The details are not given. The pattern looks like the trouble Timothy faced in Ephesus.

‘Must be silenced’ does not mean by force. It means their teaching must be stopped in the church, by elders who can answer it with the true message (verse 9), and by rebuke (verse 13).
passages.ot: The prophets spoke against those who taught for money: “Her leaders judge for a bribe, her priests teach for a price, and her prophets practice divination for money” (Micah 3:11). Isaiah described leaders who were “each one seeking his own gain” (Isaiah 56:11). And the law and Proverbs hate dishonest gain: “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 11:1).
passages.hard:
Who were ‘those of the circumcision’, and is this a word against the Jewish people?

No. This was a dispute among people inside the church about whether Gentile believers had to keep parts of the law, such as circumcision and food rules, to belong fully to God's people. Paul himself was a Jew. Titus, the man he is writing to, was a Gentile whom the apostles in Jerusalem did not require to be circumcised (Galatians 2:3). Elsewhere Paul says he would give up his own salvation for his people (Romans 9:3), and asks, ‘did God reject His people?’ and answers that he did not (Romans 11:1). He calls the law ‘holy’ (Romans 7:12). His sharp words here are aimed at teachers who, in his judgment, added conditions to God's grace and took money for it, not at Jews, not at Judaism, and not at the law as God gave it.

For centuries some Christians used words like these to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 says why.

The Bible records Paul's sharp words honestly. It does not ask us to copy them. They are no pattern for how believers speak to or about anyone.
passages.asks: Paul names teachers who unsettled households for gain. Ask whether you have ever been drawn to teaching that asked you to add something to Christ before you could belong. Ask whether anyone has made money from your faith in ways that were not right. And ask whether your words in your own home build it up or unsettle it.

passages.t: ‘Cretans are always liars’; pure and defiled
passages.happening:
Paul quotes a saying from Crete itself. “As one of their own prophets has said, ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.’ This testimony is true” (verses 12-13).

“Therefore rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith and will pay no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of men who have rejected the truth” (verses 13-14).

“To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him. They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed” (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
‘One of their own prophets’ means a Cretan. Ancient tradition says the line came from Epimenides, a Cretan poet and seer of about the 500s BC, and its opening words also appear in a later Greek poet, Callimachus. Other Greeks thought Cretans lied. Cretans claimed that the tomb of the god Zeus was on their island, and other Greeks, who believed Zeus could not die, called that a lie. They even made a verb from the island's name that meant ‘to lie’.

Paul uses the saying with some irony. A Cretan said it about Cretans. Paul turns it against particular teachers who were lying for money. And notice his goal: ‘so that they will be sound in the faith’. He wants them corrected and healed, not destroyed.

Then Paul gives a principle: ‘To the pure, all things are pure.’ The false teachers had rules about what was clean and unclean. Jesus had taught that what makes a person unclean is not what goes into the mouth, but what comes from the heart (Mark 7:18-23). A clean heart can receive God's good gifts with thanks. A dirty heart spoils everything it touches, even religion.

The last verse is the sharpest. ‘They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.’ Their words said one thing and their lives another. In Titus, faith is always seen in what people do.
passages.ot:
God made the world good: “And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31).

The psalms ask who may come near God, and answer with clean hearts and honest words: “He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:4), and “He who walks with integrity and practices righteousness, who speaks the truth from his heart” (Psalm 15:2).

Isaiah described people whose words and hearts did not match: “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me” (Isaiah 29:13). And Proverbs says that conduct shows what a person is: “Even a young man is known by his actions” (Proverbs 20:11).
passages.hard:
Paul quotes a saying that all Cretans are liars, and adds, ‘This testimony is true.’ Is he teaching that a whole people are bad by nature?

No. Paul quotes a Cretan poet against particular teachers who were lying for gain, and he does it with irony, turning a Cretan's own words on those who had earned them. His aim is their healing: ‘so that they will be sound in the faith’. He was writing to a church made up of Cretans, whom he loved enough to leave Titus with them, and to a man he trusted to lead them. And the same letter puts every believer, Paul included, in the list of those who were once ‘foolish, disobedient, misled’ until God's mercy found them (3:3).

This verse has been quoted to sneer at whole peoples, to say that some nation, race or group is lying, lazy or worse by nature. That is a misuse, and it is wrong. The Bible teaches that every person is made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), and that the gospel is for every nation. No one may use this verse to justify contempt for any people.

Notice too that Paul's harshest word is for people who ‘profess to know God, but by their actions … deny Him’. That warning points first at religious people, at us, not at outsiders.
passages.asks: Paul says some profess to know God but deny him by their actions. Ask whether your life and your words agree. Ask whether you have ever spoken of a whole group of people as if they were all one thing, and what it would mean to stop. And ask God for a clean heart that can receive his good gifts with thanks.
